title: The Periodic Table
tagline: From Dobereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves to Mendeleev's predictions and the modern law based on atomic number.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The periodic table is the organising framework of the whole subject: it arranges elements so that similar ones line up and their properties repeat periodically. This chapter follows the historical development — Dobereiner's triads, Newlands' law of octaves, Mendeleev's table and its bold predictions, and finally the modern law based on atomic number — because each step shows what a successful classification must achieve. You will then use the structure of groups and periods to explain trends in atomic size, valency and metallic character.

facts.label: Modern periodic law
facts.value: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers

facts.label: Periods
facts.value: Horizontal rows (7); elements fill shells from 1 upwards

facts.label: Groups
facts.value: Vertical columns (18 in the modern table; 1-8 in Mendeleev's numbering) with similar valency and properties

blocks.text: Before a successful table existed, chemists looked for patterns in the known elements. Dobereiner noticed triads — groups of three elements where the middle element's atomic mass was approximately the average of the other two, and its properties were intermediate: lithium, sodium and potassium form such a triad (sodium's mass 23 lies near the mean of 7 and 39). Triads worked only for a few groups and failed for many elements. Newlands went further: arranging elements in order of increasing atomic mass, he found that every eighth element resembled the first, like the octaves of a musical scale — calcium's properties repeated at scandium, eight places later. Newlands' law of octaves broke down beyond calcium because not every element obeyed the pattern, and he forced some elements into wrong positions to preserve it.

items.meaning: Three elements whose middle member has nearly the mean atomic mass and intermediate properties (Dobereiner).
Newlands' observation that every eighth element, arranged by atomic mass, resembled the first (like musical octaves).
Repeating at regular intervals — properties return to similar values as atomic mass or number increases.

items: Dobereiner's triads: a working pattern for a few groups only — not a general classification.
Newlands arranged by atomic mass and found repetition every eight places.
Newlands' law failed for elements heavier than calcium and required forcing pairs of elements into single slots.
Both attempts were limited because they used atomic mass alone and had no place for undiscovered elements.

items.text: Triad check: lithium 7, sodium 23, potassium 39. Mean of 7 and 39 is 23 — exactly sodium's mass.
items.note: Chlorine, bromine and iodine form another triad: mean of 35.5 and 127 is about 81, close to bromine's 80.

items.text: Newlands' octaves: counting from lithium — Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Na — sodium is the eighth element and resembles lithium; the same pairing gives Be-Mg, B-Al, C-Si, N-P, O-S and F-Cl.
items.note: The count starts with the element itself, as in a musical scale where the octave repeats the first note.

blocks.text: Mendeleev arranged the then-known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and grouped elements with similar chemical properties into the same vertical group, leaving gaps where no element was yet known. His periodic law stated that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. The table had eight groups (I to VIII) and seven periods, with hydrogen at the top and transition metals placed in separate series. Two features made it famous: he swapped elements where strict mass order would have ruined chemical similarity (tellurium before iodine, cobalt before nickel), and he predicted the properties of undiscovered elements — eka-aluminium (gallium, found 1875), eka-silicon (germanium, found 1886) and eka-boron (scandium, found 1879) — with such accuracy that their discovery confirmed the table.

items: Mendeleev's law: properties are a periodic function of atomic mass.
He left gaps deliberately for elements not yet discovered and described their expected properties.
Anomalies: tellurium is heavier than iodine but is placed first for chemical similarity; cobalt and nickel are similarly swapped.
Triads and octaves were special cases of Mendeleev's general pattern.
The transition elements sat in a separate inner series, which he did not force into the main groups.

items.text: Eka-aluminium: Mendeleev predicted density about 5.9 g per cm3 and oxide formula Ea2O3; gallium, discovered in 1875, has density 5.94 g per cm3 and forms Ga2O3.
items.note: Predictions of both physical constants and formulas — not just existence — are what proved the table's power.

items.text: Eka-silicon (germanium): predicted atomic mass 72, density 5.5; found values were 72.6 and 5.35.
items.note: Close agreement like this converted sceptics into supporters of the classification.

items.meaning: Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
Vertical column of elements with similar chemical properties and the same outer-electron count.
Horizontal row; elements in it successively fill the same outer shell.
Mendeleev's name for the undiscovered element below aluminium, later identified as gallium.

blocks.text: Mendeleev's mass-based law had unexplained exceptions, and the discovery of isotopes showed that atomic mass did not determine order at all: argon (39.95) precedes potassium (39.10) by mass but must follow it chemically, and no consistent mass-based arrangement fits every case. Moseley's X-ray experiments showed that the atomic number Z increases in whole-number steps across the table, and the modern periodic law therefore states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. With Z as the organising quantity, every anomaly disappears: elements are ordered by proton count, isotopes of an element occupy the same position, and the positions of argon and potassium follow their chemistry.

items: Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
Atomic number equals the number of protons, so it identifies an element unambiguously.
Isotopes have identical Z, so they occupy a single position — mass-based ordering could not do this.
In the modern table there are 18 groups and 7 periods (for the first 103+ elements).
Elements are classified as metals, non-metals or metalloids along a staircase boundary.

items.text: Argon (Z = 18, Ar = 39.95) and potassium (Z = 19, Ar = 39.10): by mass argon would come after potassium, contradicting their chemistry.
items.note: Ordered by atomic number, potassium follows argon and both fit their groups — the anomaly is resolved.

items.text: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have Z = 6, so both are carbon and both sit in the same place in the table.
items.note: A mass-based table could not place isotopes consistently; a number-based table does so naturally.

blocks.text: Reading the table structurally explains why properties recur. A period is a row: as you move left to right, one proton is added at each step and one electron goes into the same outer shell, so the increasing nuclear charge pulls the shell inward and atomic size decreases, while metallic character weakens as elements behave more like electron-gainers. A group is a column: every member has the same number of outer electrons, so valency repeats down the group, but each successive member has one more shell, so atomic size increases and the outer electrons are held less firmly, making elements more metallic. These linked trends — size, valency, metallic character — are the working tools for answering periodic questions.

items: Across a period (left to right): atomic size decreases, metallic character decreases, non-metallic character increases.
Down a group: atomic size increases (more shells), metallic character increases, valency stays the same.
Valency across period 3 rises from 1 (Na) to 4 (Si) then falls: 1 (P), 2 (S), 1 (Cl) — because valency relates to electrons gained or shared to complete the octet.
Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, hence similar formulas of compounds: NaCl, KCl; Li2O, K2O.
Noble gases (group 18/0) have full outer shells, so they are inert.

items.text: Chlorine (2, 8, 7) and bromine (2, 8, 18, 7) both have 7 outer electrons, so both form ions with 1- charge and compounds like NaCl and NaBr.
items.note: Same group, same valency, similar formulas — the clearest evidence of periodicity.

items.text: Sodium (2, 8, 1) to chlorine (2, 8, 7) across period 3: size falls, metallic character falls, and the elements change from reactive metal to reactive non-metal.
items.note: One trend statement per step earns the marks; always say what increases and what decreases.

items.meaning: Horizontal row; filling of the same outer shell occurs across it.
Vertical column; elements share outer-electron count, valency and formula patterns.
Tendency to lose electrons; increases down a group and decreases across a period.
Decreases across a period (stronger nuclear pull) and increases down a group (new shells).

figures.caption: Figure: Reading trends on the table
figures.description: Arrow right across a period: atomic size down, metallic character down, non-metallicity up. Arrow down a group: atomic size up, metallic character up, valency unchanged.

keyPoints: Dobereiner's triads: middle element has near-average mass and intermediate properties.
Newlands: every eighth element resembled the first when arranged by mass — valid only up to calcium.
Mendeleev arranged by atomic mass, left gaps, predicted new elements, and prioritised chemical similarity over strict mass order.
Mendeleev's anomalies: Te before I; Co before Ni.
Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
Isotopes and the argon-potassium order are explained only by the atomic-number law.
Across a period: size and metallic character decrease; down a group: size and metallic character increase.
Same group means same outer-electron count and similar valency and formulas.
examFocus: History questions expect names plus the specific rule each chemist proposed — 'he classified elements' earns little without the rule.
For prediction questions, quote both the predicted value and the discovered value to show agreement.
When asked why atomic number replaced atomic mass, cite isotopes and the argon-potassium anomaly.
Trend answers must state direction explicitly: 'decreases across a period because added nuclear charge pulls the shell inward'.

vocabulary.meaning: Three elements with middle member of average mass and similar properties.
Newlands' rule that every eighth element repeats the first's properties.
Properties repeat periodically with atomic number (modern) or mass (Mendeleev).
Vertical column with shared valency and chemistry.
Horizontal row corresponding to filling one outer shell.

questions.explanation: In a triad the middle element's atomic mass is close to the average of the other two — the pattern was mass-based.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing atomic number, which was not known in Dobereiner's time.

questions.prompt: Newlands' law of octaves worked only up to:
questions.explanation: Beyond calcium, every eighth element no longer resembled the first, and Newlands had to force elements into pairs to keep the pattern.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing sodium (the start of his second row) with calcium (the limit of the pattern).

questions.prompt: Mendeleev's table differed from earlier attempts because he:
options: Left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements
questions.answer: Left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements
questions.explanation: Deliberate gaps for undiscovered elements, with predicted properties later confirmed, distinguished his table; atomic-number ordering came later with Moseley.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing atomic number — Mendeleev used atomic mass and only the modern law uses Z.

questions.prompt: The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of:
questions.explanation: Moseley showed that atomic number, not mass, governs the order; this resolved anomalies such as argon before potassium.
questions.commonMistake: Quoting Mendeleev's mass-based law when the question specifies the MODERN law.

questions.prompt: Moving from left to right across a period, atomic size:
options: Increases, because more electrons join the outer shell
Decreases, because nuclear charge increases without a new shell
questions.answer: Decreases, because nuclear charge increases without a new shell
questions.explanation: Each step adds a proton and an electron in the SAME outer shell; the stronger pull draws the shell closer.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking added electrons enlarge the atom — they add to the same shell while nuclear charge rises.

questions.prompt: Elements in the same group have the same:
questions.explanation: Group membership is defined by identical outer-electron count, which gives the same valency and similar chemistry.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing number of shells — that is what varies DOWN a group.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Mendeleev predicted an element he called ________, which was later discovered and named ________.
questions.explanation: Eka-aluminium sat below aluminium in his table; gallium, discovered in 1875, matched the predicted density and oxide formula.
questions.commonMistake: Pairing eka-silicon with germanium instead — eka-aluminium is the gallium case.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: tellurium is placed BEFORE iodine in the periodic table although tellurium has the greater atomic mass, because Mendeleev prioritised ________ over strict mass order.
questions.explanation: Both elements belong with the group of similar non-metals; swapping them would have ruined the chemical pattern of the columns.
questions.commonMistake: Saying he made an error — the swap was deliberate and later justified by the atomic-number ordering (I, Z = 53, follows Te, Z = 52).

questions.prompt: State two limitations of Newlands' law of octaves and explain how Mendeleev overcame each.
questions.answer: Limitation 1: the pattern held only up to calcium — heavier elements did not repeat every eighth place. Mendeleev produced a table for all known elements with groups based on similarity rather than a fixed numerical repeat. Limitation 2: Newlands forced pairs of elements into one slot and had no gaps for undiscovered elements. Mendeleev left deliberate gaps and predicted the properties of the missing elements, later confirmed by discovery.
questions.explanation: Each limitation is answered by a specific feature of Mendeleev's table: general grouping and purposeful gaps.
questions.commonMistake: Listing limitations without the matching Mendeleev solution, which the question explicitly pairs.

questions.prompt: Explain why the discovery of isotopes created a problem for Mendeleev's periodic law but not for the modern one.
questions.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different atomic masses but identical atomic numbers. Mendeleev's law ordered elements by atomic mass, so isotopes of different elements could interleave and demand different positions for the same element — an internal contradiction. The modern law orders by atomic number, and all isotopes of an element share the same Z, so the element occupies exactly one position regardless of its isotopes.
questions.explanation: The problem is specific to mass-based ordering; number-based ordering is immune because Z is invariant for an element.
questions.commonMistake: Saying isotopes have different properties — their chemistry is identical; the difficulty is one of ordering, not behaviour.

questions.prompt: Describe how metallic character varies (a) across period 3 from sodium to chlorine and (b) down group 1 from lithium to caesium, and explain both trends.
questions.answer: (a) Across period 3 metallic character decreases: sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine a reactive non-metal. Each step adds a proton and an electron to the same shell, so the nucleus holds electrons more firmly and atoms lose them less easily. (b) Down group 1 metallic character increases: each element has one more shell than the one above, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and held less firmly, making it easier to lose.
questions.explanation: Metallic character means readiness to lose electrons; anything that makes the outer electron easier to lose increases it.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the across-period trend by reasoning that 'more electrons means more metallic' — the nuclear pull on the same shell dominates.

questions.prompt: Write an account of Mendeleev's periodic law, its two celebrated strengths, and the two anomalies that later required the modern law.
questions.answer: Mendeleev's law: the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. Strength 1: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties — eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium) were later found with properties matching his predictions closely in density, oxide formula and atomic mass. Strength 2: he prioritised chemical similarity, placing elements in families whose patterns allowed valid generalisations about compounds and valency. Anomaly 1: some elements were out of mass order — tellurium before iodine, cobalt before nickel — with no mass-based explanation. Anomaly 2: isotopes showed that the same element can have different masses, so mass cannot be the true ordering quantity, and the apparent mass conflict between argon and potassium could not be resolved. The modern law, ordering by atomic number, removed both anomalies.
questions.explanation: The full answer links the law, its predictive success, its internal inconsistencies, and why atomic number is the correct variable.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the successes — the question explicitly asks for the anomalies, and omitting them loses half the marks.

questions.prompt: Why does valency remain constant down a group but change across a period?
questions.answer: Valency depends on the number of outer electrons available for sharing or transfer. Down a group, every element has the same number of outer electrons — group 1 has one, group 17 has seven — so valency is unchanged even though shells are added. Across a period, outer electrons increase one by one in the same shell, so the number of electrons gained, lost or shared to reach an octet changes step by step: valency rises to four and then falls as elements switch from losing to gaining electrons.
questions.explanation: Group = same outer count = same valency; period = changing outer count = changing valency. The distinction follows directly from how the table is built.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming valency is always 1, 2 or 3 down a group without reference to outer-electron counts (nitrogen family reaches valency 3 by sharing, phosphorus also shows valency 5 in some compounds).
